The 1930s depression stifled the demand for lime, but Bayview’s kilns operated sporadically until 1941.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Burke
text:
Located in a narrow canyon, builders in Burke faced unique challenges. When S.S. Glidden built a hotel, he named it for his nearby Tiger-Poorman Mine. Confined by the steep topography, the Tiger Hotel had to span both railroad tracks and Canyon Creek.  Locals claimed it was the only such hotel in the world.

The hotel’s last owner razed it in 1954. The last Burke mine closed in 1991.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Coeur d'Alene Lake
text: An ice dam at Lake Pend Oreille blocked the Clark Fork River, creating Lake Missoula, larger than the state of Delaware. It ruptured periodically, releasing torrents of water carrying boulders and gravel that sometimes formed smaller dams downstream, turning valleys into lakes. Here, the Coeur d’Alene and St. Joe Rivers flooded a former valley, creating Coeur d’Alene Lake. At 32,000 acres, with 109 miles of shoreline, many consider it one of the world’s most beautiful lakes.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: David Thompson (1770-1857)
text:
On May 8, 1808, Thompson’s famished party met ten lodges of Kootenai people near here. Short of food themselves, the Kootenai nonetheless offered fish and “moss bread,” made from tree lichens. Thompson termed the bread “slightly bitter…but acceptable to the hungry.” He called the place Camp Providence.

Thompson left on an established Indian trail, the same route US Highway 95 now follows. In 1809, he returned to Camp Providence. Kootenai people guided him to Lake Pend Oreille, where he established Idaho’s first fur-trading post.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: DeSmet (‘l’lkhwi’lus)
text: Nineteenth century federal policy sought to assimilate Indians into white culture. Christian mission boarding schools like the one at DeSmet helped accomplish this, but at a cost. Children were separated from families and had to relinquish traditional clothing, religious practices, and native language. The original DeSmet mission and school buildings are gone. The Schitsu’umsh, a sovereign nation with an elected government, replaced the boarding school with a tribal school in the 1990s.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Farragut
text: Built inland to protect against possible Japanese coastal invasions, it became Idaho’s largest community and America’s second-largest naval training center. Nearly 300,000 sailors prepared here. It also served briefly as a German prisoner of war camp, and from 1946-49, Farragut College and Technical Institute. In 1965, it became Farragut State Park. With 4,000 acres, it has hosted jamborees attracting thousands of Boy and Girl Scouts from around the world, as well as visitors who enjoy its stunning lakeshore setting.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Mining Wars
text:
After mine owners increased work hours and cut wages, a gunfight erupted between workers and company guards. Miners blew up the Frisco Mill near here. Five men died. Federal troops incarcerated miners. Grievances lingered. On April 29, 1899, miners hijacked a train. Loading it with dynamite here, they destroyed Wardner’s Bunker Hill mill. Two more died. Governor Frank Stuenenberg declared martial law. Federal troops again incarcerated miners. 

The conflict fostered formation of the Western Federation of Miners union, Idaho’s eight-hour workday, and former Governor Steunenberg’s 1905 assassination.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: 25th Infantry Regiment
text: In Wallace, the 25th maintained order as flames descended on the town, then evacuated women and children on outbound trains. In Avery, the troops helped residents escape and lit backfires that saved the community. The regiment also built trails for fire crews and retrieved bodies from burned areas. “The soldiers of the 25th Infantry have done heroic service and saved many lives and much property,” reported the Seattle Times.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: John Mullan (1830-1909) (After the Road)
text: After roadbuilding, Mullan’s life proved less gratifying. In 1863, he resigned from the Army and attempted unsuccessfully to gain President Lincoln’s appointment as Idaho’s first territorial governor. He then failed as a Walla Walla businessman and as partner in a Boise-to-California stage line. He finally found success as a California lawyer, but eventually lost his fortune. He died penniless in 1909, the year automobiles first traveled his road.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Bunker Hill Mine
text: Bunker Hill produced more than 30 million tons of lead, silver, and zinc, built the world’s largest smelter, and employed thousands. The smelter also released sulfur and lead dioxides into the air, while Bunker Hill and other mines discharged wastes into streams. In 1983, the Environmental Protection Agency began supervising the cleanup around Bunker Hill, with mining companies adapting to new environmental regulations.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Kootenai Tribe of Idaho
text: An ancient and unique culture, the Kootenai speak a language unlike any other in the world and are known for their sturgeon-nose canoes and flat bows made of yew. Despite several attempts at removal, the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho refused to leave their homes near Bonners Ferry and move to a reservation, resulting in years of hardship. In 1974, the population of the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho was 67 people. In desperation, they declared war against the United States and successfully secured a land base and federal recognition.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Kullyspel House
text: Located 2 ½ miles from here, Kullyspel House (Thompson’s spelling for Kalispel) was the first structure built by non-Indians in Idaho. A geographer and surveyor of rare skill, Thompson explored and documented vast regions for the North West Company of Montreal. Reaching south from present-day British Columbia, he extended his company’s trade influence to north Idaho. Thompson first mapped the route that Idaho Highway 200 now follows. The North West Company abandoned Kullyspel House in 1811.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: McCroskey State Park
text: A local pharmacist and conservationist, McCroskey often hiked these woods. In the 1930s, he began purchasing property to prevent logging. He stitched together a narrow strip of land and constructed a road he called Skyline Drive, with expansive views of farms and mountains. Twice he offered it to Idaho as a park. The legislature declined. In 1955, the state finally accepted his 4,400-acre donation, provided he maintain it for 15 years. McCroskey did, even purchasing additional park property. He died in 1970 at age 93. Mary Minerva McCroskey State Park honors his mother.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Lake Steamers
text:
It began in 1880, when the Army launched the Amelia Wheaton to carry supplies for Fort Coeur d’Alene (later named Fort Sherman). Many other steamers followed, hauling freight, towing logs, and carrying passengers. Docks lined the City of Coeur d’Alene’s lakefront. 

In 1927, officials burned the Georgie Oakes, “Queen of the Lake,” as part of Coeur d’Alene’s July 4th celebration. Although a few steamers operated into the 1940s, Coeur d’Alene’s steamboat era had reached its turning point.
route: E Coeur D'Alene Lake Dr (S of Coeur D'Alene)
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Schitsu'umsh
text:
French fur traders called them “Coeur d’Alene,” meaning “heart of the awl,” for their shrewd bartering skills—a name the Tribe also proudly recognizes. That keen business sense has carried on to the present. The Tribe is one of the region’s largest employers, involved in gaming, recreation, agriculture, and technology. 

The Schitsu’umsh of today are the sum of untold generations that have lived in this land of abundant beauty, rich in resources. They are who they always were and who they will always be.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Long Bridges
text: In 1910, contractors sank 1,540 pilings to support a two-mile-long wagon bridge. Locals claimed it the longest wooden bridge in the world. A new automobile bridge replaced the wagon structure in the 1930s, and in the 1950s a concrete and steel span connected the two towns. That bridge remains, a popular walking and biking path that parallels the latest Long Bridge, completed in 1981.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Dawes Act
text:
Schitsu’umsh in the DeSmet area grew wheat, potatoes, oats, and hay—among the most successful Northwest Indian farmers. The Dawes Act, which sought to encourage farming by allotting land to individual tribal members, actually failed the Schitsu’umsh. 

Implementation began here in 1909. Federal agents assigned 160 acres to tribal members, shrinking many Schitsu’umsh farms to economically inviable sizes. Non-Indians purchased the “surplus” property. Schitsu’umsh lost thousands of acres. The Tribe now works now to buy back lost lands.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Mullan Road
text: From 1858-62, John Mullan's Army road crew built the Northwest's first engineered highway, connecting Fort Benton with Fort Walla Walla, 625 miles long. Idaho’s portion of Interstate 90—the “Captain John Mullan Highway”—roughly follows that road. Mullan's crew spent Independence Day 1861 here, giving Fourth of July Summit its name. They carved that date into a white pine. The famed Mullan Tree became a popular tourist stop before foresters removed the diseased tree in 1988.
route: I-90 (E Alder Creek Rd, Near Exit 28)
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Land of the Schitsu'umsh (Schitsu'umshu'lmkhw)
text:
Schitsu’umshu’lmkhw spanned from eastern Washington, across Idaho’s panhandle, to western Montana. In 1873, President Ulysses Grant created the Coeur d’Alene Reservation. Smaller than the Tribe’s ancestral lands, it was still huge. The discovery of gold in the Silver Valley brought widespread trespassing onto the reservation. In the 1880s, Congress opened hundreds of square miles of formerly reserved lands to white settlement, shrinking the reservation to its current size.

Schitsu’umsh still hunt the forests, travel the rivers, and camp on land that has been theirs since time immemorial.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Old Mission of the Sacred Heart (sq’wt’u)
text:
Schitsu’umsh (Coeur d’Alene) tribal members undertook most of the construction for this Jesuit mission church. They quarried local fieldstone for the foundation, felled trees for beams and posts, and, using traditional techniques, wove grass through willow saplings for the walls. The site also included a barn, stable, flourmill, houses, and shops. Schitsu’umsh lodges stood near the river. 

President Ulysses Grant created the Schitsu’umsh reservation in 1873. Its boundaries excluded the mission, so Schitsu’umsh and Jesuits moved south to DeSmet. In 2001, the Boise Diocese deeded the mission to the Schitsu’umsh.
route: I-90 (Old Mission State Park, Near Exit 39)
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Pen d'Oreille City
text: The Oregon Steam Navigation Company (OSN) launched the steamboat Mary Moody, providing an alternative to the difficult land route to mines in Canada and Montana. Operating from Pen d’Oreille City, the boat shortened miners’ trips by a couple days. At its peak, the “city” had 25 residents, a store, and a saloon. Soon, the population shrank to one boat tender. When OSN dismantled the Mary Moody in 1876, Pen d’Oreille City disappeared altogether.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Rathdrum Prairie
text:
Some 15,000 years ago, a lobe of the Cordilleran ice sheet crept south from Canada to Sandpoint. The ice formed a dam creating glacial Lake Missoula, containing as much water as Lakes Erie and Ontario combined. As the climate warmed, the dam failed multiple times, repeatedly emptying the lake. Torrents of water rushed through here. The Missoula Floods shaped much of the Northwest.

Following those deluges, this lowland became a natural transportation corridor. People traveled along the valley at least 10,000 years ago. Today, highways run through it.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Saint Joseph Mission (St'uts'te'wes)
text:
In 1842, Jesuits established Idaho’s first Catholic mission here. To encourage Schitsu’umsh to farm, the Jesuits prohibited fish trapping. Ignoring Schitsu’umsh advice, the Jesuits constructed a small church and other buildings near the river. As tribal members had predicted, spring floods ravaged the structures and destroyed much of the farmland. After subsisting a winter on barley soup, the Jesuits relented, collaborating with Schitsu’umsh to build a new fish trap utilizing construction methods from both cultures. 

In 1846, Jesuits left this challenging location and established a new mission at today’s Cataldo.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Submerged Valley
text: North of here near Sandpoint, the Cordilleran ice sheet blocked valleys and formed large ice-dammed lakes. Repeated failures of the dams drained the lakes. Waters rushed across the outlet of this valley, beyond modern Coeur d’Alene. Sand and gravel deposited there raised the level of the land and blocked the old river channel. This backed up the river, submerged the valley before you, and produced one of Idaho’s lovely landscapes.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Seneacquoteen
text: In 1811, Canadian fur trader David Thompson crossed ntxwe  here, and in 1860-61, international boundary survey teams established base camps on the river’s banks. Gold rushes in Montana and Canada later brought thousands of miners. Starting in 1864, a ferry provided transport. By then, Seneacquoteen had a couple saloons and stores. For a time, it was the seat of Kootenai County government. When the Northern Pacific Railroad bypassed Seneacquoteen, its brief boom faded, but the ferry operated until 1957.
route: Parking area at end of Laclede Ferry Rd (off SH-2)
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Sunshine Mine Disaster
text:
On May 2, fire broke out a half mile underground at the nearby Sunshine Mine. Heat, smoke, and gas spread quickly through the intricate system of underground workings. Of the 173 workers who entered the mine that day, 91 died—all from carbon monoxide poisoning.

This Idaho tragedy helped transform the nation’s mining industry, prompting passage of the federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977. The act brought stricter safety regulations—including rescue training and evacuation drills—that continue to govern hard-rock mining.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Mullan Road
text:
In an Army display of power, Colonel Edward Steptoe marched 158 troops out of Fort Walla Walla. Schitsu’umsh and other warriors routed him at today’s Rosalia, Washington. Later, Colonel George Wright brutally avenged Steptoe’s defeat and forced tribes to accept road construction. 

Mullan initially built his road nearby in 1859. After it flooded, he charted a different route northwest of here. Completed in 1862, Mullan’s road connected the Missouri and Columbia Rivers. It brought settlers to the Northwest while transforming tribal lifeways.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Treaty Rock (q’emiln)
text: Despite popular legend, Post and Seltice never signed a treaty here. Some of the markings on nearby Treaty Rock might pre-date 1871; others probably came later to commemorate the negotiations. But undisputed is the enduring legacy of Post and the Seltice family. The waterfall Post acquired powered his sawmill—this region’s first. He also platted this town bearing his name. Numerous place names in Washington, Idaho, and Montana—Seltice or Saltese—bear witness to that family’s significance.
route: N Compton, Post Falls (Treaty Rock Park, off I-90)
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Wallace
text: Wallace has retained a large number of historic buildings reflecting its mining past. As engineers designed the Interstate 90 expansion, the original plan took the highway through town, requiring the removal of much of the pristine architecture. The community successfully argued for an alternative. In 1991, Wallace ceremonially retired the last stoplight on the 3,000-mile Interstate 90—as the new freeway bypassed the town.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Bonners Ferry
text:
In 1864, British Columbia’s Kootenay gold rush drew miners to Canada. Steamboats began working the river in the 1880s; railroads arrived in the 1890s. Area forests attracted lumber companies, and the fertile river valley brought farmers. Bonners Ferry—then in Bonner County—became a commercial hub. 

In 1915, Idaho’s legislature carved Boundary County out of Bonner County. Ironically, the county named for Ed Bonner’s ferry now lies south of here, and Bonners Ferry is the governmental seat of Boundary County.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Willow Creek Slide
text: The engine plunged 80 feet, sinking into 30 feet of snow. A passenger car dangled precariously over the open gap. The caboose tumbled into a deep snowbank. Though it took 11 hours to free injured workers, everyone aboard the train miraculously survived the terror-stricken trip. A new, less hazardous grade replaced the demolished trestle.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Chinese Railroad Workers
text:
In 1881-82, nearly 6,000 workers laid Northern Pacific Railroad track along northern Lake Pend Oreille, the most difficult and costly construction on the entire route. They worked here in winter, removing up to seven feet of snow just to reach ground level. 

Chinese immigrants accounted for two-thirds of the labor force. They lived and worked separately from others, often undertaking the most arduous and dangerous tasks. Following construction, some Chinese remained as section crews. The nearby town of Hope had a Chinese community well into the 20th century.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Mary Allen Wright (1868-1948)
text:
Wright, an ardent suffragist, moved from Washington to Rathdrum in 1890. In 1898, Idahoans elected three women legislators, a Republican, a Democrat, and Populist Mary Wright. She chaired the Populist Caucus, the first woman nationally to lead a state legislative party. 

Wright served one term, divorced, and moved to Bonners Ferry in 1912, where she managed Wright’s Loan and Investment Company. One of America’s trailblazing women politicians, she died here in 1948.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Gladys Buroker (1914-2002)
text: During the war, Gladys and husband Herb operated from Coeur d’Alene’s Weeks Field. Gladys trained military pilots; Herb maintained the planes. In the 1970s, the Burokers, along with partner Clay Henley, opened Henley Aerodrome near Athol. Gladys gave flying lessons and entertained visitors with hot-air balloon rides. Gary Norton purchased the Aerodrome in 1981. It gradually evolved into Silverwood Theme Park. Gladys stayed on, managing the airfield for Silverwood’s acclaimed air shows. She retired in 1990 but continued flying well into her 80s.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Submarine Testing
text: During World War II, the Farragut Naval Training Station prepared nearly 300,000 sailors for duty. Following the war, the Navy retained a 25-acre parcel of the former training center for its Acoustic Research Detachment (ARD). As the nation’s fifth-deepest lake, Pend Oreille proved an ideal submarine testing environment. With a fleet of reduced-scale submarines, ARD undertakes trials here at a fraction of the expense of ocean research, aiding the Navy’s development of efficient, quiet submarines. The ARD’s Bayview base has supported nearly every major post-World War II submarine design.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Levi and May Hutton
text:
May Arkwright owned a Wardner boarding house. Levi Hutton, a locomotive engineer, dined there regularly. After marrying in 1887, they invested their modest savings in the Hercules. In 1901, the partners struck a fabulously rich silver vein. 

May devoted much of her new prosperity to supporting women’s suffrage. The Huttons also donated generously to philanthropy. After May died in 1915, Levi purchased 111 acres east of Spokane and founded the Hutton Settlement for orphans. He died in 1928, bequeathing his fortune to the Settlement, which still exists.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Restoring the Lake
text: This beautiful lake has always been a center of Schitsu’umsh (Coeur d’Alene) life. In 1991, the Tribe filed one of the largest natural resource lawsuits in American history in an effort to compel a lake cleanup. A far-reaching legal victory resulted in mining companies paying millions of dollars to mitigate damages. The Tribe, along with federal and state agencies, began the long-term project of restoring the lake.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Joseph Garry (1910-1975)
text: Garry served on the Schitsu’umsh (Coeur d’Alene) Tribal Council for 25 years, and was the first Indian elected to the Idaho House of Representatives (1956) and Senate (1966). In 1953, the National Congress of American Indians elected him president. That year, Congress resolved to terminate federal tribal recognition and assimilate Indians by moving them off reservations. Garry rallied tribes throughout the country to Washington, DC, “the biggest demonstration by Indians ever” in that city. Garry’s gathering triggered a successful, multi-year effort to defeat termination.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

title: Bannock War
text: The war had begun in June on Camas Prairie and had swung clear to central Oregon. Now the Indians were returning to their reservation at Fort Hall. Harried from the island, they soon lost the pursuing troops in rough country north of here. This was the last battle of the war.
source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society
